intro.heading: The photo is in the building. Nobody can find it.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Mrs Dunn gets restless around four every afternoon. Today the carer with her is Priya, who started on the unit on Monday. The key worker said Mrs Dunn loves talking about her wedding, and that her son had brought in a few photos. Priya has no idea where they are. They might be in a drawer, in a folder on the office computer, or still in the son's message thread. The unit is busy, and Priya does not want to leave Mrs Dunn alone while she hunts for them.

trail.text: Mrs Dunn becomes restless and starts to look for the door.
Priya sits with her and speaks calmly.
Priya remembers the key worker mentioning the wedding photos.
She cannot find them. They may be in a drawer or on a phone.
She asks a colleague. Nobody is sure who has them.
The same thing happens again, with a different carer.
The son asks if the photos have been any use. Nobody knows.
“How do you know what matters to her?” A drawer is not an answer.

trail_close: The photos were there. The gap is between having them and finding the right one in the moment. Here is how CareStream gets approved photos in front of the carer who needs them.

why.heading: Why the right photo matters in the moment
why.sub: Familiar faces and places can help someone feel safe, when words do not.

cards.title: A photo gives staff something to say
cards.body: Formal and everyday reminiscence both start with something familiar to talk about. A carer new to the unit can say, “Is that your wedding day?” and let the person lead.

cards.title: It is part of person centred care
cards.body: Care must reflect the person's preferences, and where someone cannot decide for themselves the Mental Capacity Act asks you to consider their past and present wishes and feelings. Knowing who and what matters is where it begins.

cards.title: Finding it is the hard part
cards.body: Photos in drawers, on phones and in folders are hard to find at four o'clock. And a carer should not have to pass round a photo that nobody has checked.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: How does a carer find a photo of a resident?
items.a: They open the This is me chat in the Staff Hub and ask, for example, whether there is a photo of the person's wedding. The chat answers, and approved photos that match appear as small pictures under the answer. A tap makes one bigger.

items.q: How does it know which photo is the wedding?
items.a: From the captions and notes people wrote, matched by meaning. A caption that says “married” will be found by a question about a wedding. It does not look inside a picture. If no caption matches, it shows that person's photos and says none is captioned that way.

No. CareStream helps staff find an approved photo quickly. What the carer does with it, from a quiet chat to a planned reminiscence session, is up to your team and your own approach. Nothing here is clinical advice.

items.q: Who decides which photos staff can see?
items.a: A manager. Every family photo waits for approval on the Approvals tab, and you can edit the caption first or reject it. Photos you add yourself from the record are approved at once.

items.q: What if a resident does not want to see a photo?
items.a: Then the carer does not use it. A photo is a way in to a conversation, not a requirement. Staff need to read the person, and your own care plan and the person's wishes come first.

items.q: What if the question does not name the resident?
items.a: If several residents have photos, the chat asks who is meant before it shows anything.

items.q: What happens when someone moves on or passes away?
items.a: Their photos leave the hub straight away. Approved files stay in private storage for the retention period, like the written profile, then are deleted with it.

items.q: Which plan is it on, and can I try it?
items.a: Resident profiles and photos are on Professional and above. There is a 14 day free trial, and the pricing page shows which plan includes it. You can create an account or book a demo to see it first.

limits.heading: Honest limits: a way to find the photo, not a therapy

cards.title: It reads captions, not pictures
cards.body: The chat cannot see inside a photo or describe what is in it. A photo with no useful caption is hard to find by a question, so good captions matter. Photos and captions are not used for the chat's other answers.

cards.title: It does not run a session
cards.body: CareStream does not plan, deliver or record reminiscence work, and it does not give clinical advice. It helps a carer find an approved photo. The rest is your team's judgement and the person's choice.

cards.title: It depends on approval
cards.body: A photo only appears once a manager has approved it, so someone needs to check the Approvals tab. It is on Professional and above, and the family cannot see the profile or message you.

faqs.heading: Photos, the chat and reminiscence, answered

items.q: What is reminiscence therapy for dementia?
items.a: It generally means helping someone talk about their past, often with photos, music or objects they know. CareStream does not provide it. It helps staff find approved photos for the person, as part of how your team already works. Read more in our guide to the this is me document.

items.q: What is the difference between reminiscence therapy and an everyday chat about the past?
items.a: A planned session is usually led by someone trained to run it. An everyday chat is a carer using what they know about the person. A found photo can support either, and your own approach decides which.

items.q: How does this support person centred care?
items.a: It puts what family and managers know about the person in front of the carer at the moment they need it. That includes names, places and stories. It sits beside the care plan, not in place of it.

items.q: Can the chat describe a photo?
items.a: No. It finds photos from the captions and notes, and shows them. It does not look inside a picture.

items.q: Does the chat show photos that are still waiting for approval?
items.a: No. Staff and the chat see only approved photos of current residents.
Privately. Staff see them through short lived links when signed in, and there is no public web address. Each photo is checked, scanned and saved again without location data.

items.q: Which photo will it show if I ask for a person's holiday?
items.a: The approved photos whose captions or notes match by meaning, such as a caption about Whitby. If none match, it shows that person's photos and says none is captioned that way.

items.q: Do we have to use photos?
items.a: No. Photos are optional for each resident. Where there are none, the chat answers from the written profile as usual. See resident knowledge for more.

guide.heading: How to use photos well with a person living with dementia
guide.lede: A photo is a way in, not a test. A few habits help staff use it kindly: choose the moment, follow the person, and keep the captions clear.

paragraphs: The chat finds photos by their words. Ask relatives for a few plain words and the names of the people in the photo, such as “Wedding day, 1962” or “Whitby with Joan”. Edit any caption before you approve it.

sections.h3: Before you use a photo with someone
paragraphs: Read the person's profile first, and follow their lead. Some photos bring comfort and some bring sadness. The person's wishes and your own policies come first. You can read what the regulation expects in regulation 9 on person-centred care.
checklist: Have I read what the profile says helps this person?
Is the photo one the person is likely to enjoy?
Am I ready to put it away if it upsets them?
Will I note what happened in the usual way?

sections.h3: Help new staff get the habit
paragraphs: Show new and agency staff how to ask the chat in their first shift. A dementia awareness course helps them see why a familiar photo can matter, and the Mental Capacity Act course covers wishes and best interests.

guide.note: This page describes how the software works and is not legal or clinical advice. Check your own policies and local guidance for how you use photos and reminiscence with residents.
